evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acne vulgaris: severity grading, skin care, referral triggers, first-line 12-week treatment options, review, oral isotretinoin, PMOS-related acne, relapse, maintenance and scarring. Verified against NICE NG198 (updated August 2026) and FDA labels; Saudi-specific isotretinoin requirements not checked.
findings: NICE NG198 recommendations (last updated 3 August 2026), Table 1 and Terms used were read in full on 13 Oct 2026; doses and contraindications were read from US FDA labels via openFDA on the same date.
NG198 is a UK guideline; its isotretinoin requirements refer to the UK MHRA, not Saudi regulators.
unverifiedSections: SFDA registration and the SFDA isotretinoin prescribing requirements not checked (the SFDA site refused automated access from the authoring environment)
No Saudi acne guideline was found; none is cited
Pathophysiology beyond the points in NG198's recommendations is not covered because the guideline recommendations do not describe it
Dose for oral prednisolone with isotretinoin, and for co-cyprindiol, is not stated in NG198 and is not reproduced
Lymecycline, clindamycin combinations and tretinoin products have no FDA label read here
FDA labels are US labels; Saudi product information may differ

pathophysiology.summary: Acne vulgaris is graded on a continuum by lesion counts. This topic covers adults; NICE NG198 sets age limits for some treatments, such as under 12 years for oral lymecycline or doxycycline combinations. Treatment aims to clear lesions in 12-week courses, limit scarring and psychological harm, and avoid antibiotic overuse.
keyMechanisms: Severity runs along a continuum: mild to moderate acne has any number of comedones, up to 34 inflammatory lesions, or up to 2 nodules; moderate to severe acne has 35 or more inflammatory lesions or 3 or more nodules (NICE NG198, Terms used).
The risk of scarring increases with the severity and duration of acne, and persistent picking or scratching of lesions increases it further (NICE NG198 Recs 1.2.4 and 1.5.6).
A medical disorder or medication, including self-administered anabolic steroids, may contribute to acne (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.6).
Acne with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) with extra features of hyperandrogenism needs endocrine assessment (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.31–1.5.32).
Acne of any severity can cause psychological distress and mental health disorders (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.4).

references.title: NICE NG198: Acne vulgaris: management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendations 1.2.4, 1.4.6, 1.5.4, 1.5.6 and 1.5.31–1.5.32; Terms used in this guideline

symptoms: Non-inflammatory lesions (comedones) and inflammatory lesions (NICE NG198, Terms used).
Nodules; acne may affect hard-to-reach areas such as the back (NICE NG198 Terms used and Table 1).
Psychological distress, which can occur at any severity (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.4).
Scarring and persistent pigmentary changes (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.3 and 1.8.1).
physicalSigns: Count of inflammatory lesions and nodules to grade severity: mild to moderate up to 34 inflammatory lesions or up to 2 nodules; moderate to severe 35 or more inflammatory lesions or 3 or more nodules (NICE NG198, Terms used).
Acne conglobata: a severe form of nodulo-cystic acne with interconnecting sinuses and abscesses (NICE NG198, Terms used).
Acne fulminans: a very serious form of acne conglobata associated with systemic symptoms (NICE NG198, Terms used).
redFlags: Acne fulminans: refer the same day to the on-call hospital dermatology team, to be assessed within 24 hours (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.1).
Acne conglobata or nodulo-cystic acne, or diagnostic uncertainty: refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.2).
Suicidal ideation or self-harm, a severe depressive or anxiety disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder: consider referral to mental health services (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.5).
Pregnancy or planned pregnancy while on topical retinoids, oral tetracyclines or isotretinoin (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.8 and 1.5.22).
precipitants: A medical disorder or medication, including self-administered anabolic steroids (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.6).
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (formerly polycystic ovary syndrome) (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.31).
Oil-based and comedogenic skin care, sunscreens and make-up (NICE NG198 Recs 1.2.2–1.2.3).
Persistent picking or scratching of lesions increases scarring risk (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.2.4).
NICE finds not enough evidence to support specific diets for acne (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.3.1).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Severe nodulo-cystic acne with interconnecting sinuses and abscesses; refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198 Terms used and Rec. 1.4.2).
Very serious form of acne conglobata with systemic symptoms; same-day referral to the on-call hospital dermatology team (NICE NG198 Terms used and Rec. 1.4.1).

differentials.condition: Acne due to a medical disorder or medication
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: A disorder or drug, including self-administered anabolic steroids, is likely contributing; consider condition-specific management or specialist referral (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.6).

differentials.condition: Acne with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and hyperandrogenism
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acne with PMOS plus additional features of hyperandrogenism; consider referral to a specialist such as a reproductive endocrinologist (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.31–1.5.32).
NG198 lists no specific alternative diagnoses; diagnostic uncertainty is itself a reason to refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.2).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Mild to moderate acne (NICE NG198, Terms used)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Any number of comedones, up to 34 inflammatory lesions, or up to 2 nodules

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Moderate to severe acne (NICE NG198, Terms used)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 35 or more inflammatory lesions (with or without comedones) or 3 or more nodules

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: First-line course and review (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.1 and 1.5.12)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 12-week course of one first-line option, reviewed at 12 weeks; positive effects take 6 to 8 weeks to become noticeable

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Referral after treatment failure (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.3 and 1.5.17)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Mild to moderate acne not responding to 2 completed courses; moderate to severe acne not responding to treatment that contained an oral antibiotic

Older than 12 years with severe acne resistant to adequate courses of standard systemic antibiotic and topical therapy, for example nodulo-cystic acne, acne conglobata, acne fulminans or acne at risk of permanent scarring

Standard 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily; below 0.5 mg/kg if at increased risk of adverse effects; continue to a cumulative dose of 120 to 150 mg/kg, or stop earlier after adequate response and no new lesions for 4 to 8 weeks
Beyond 6 months only in exceptional circumstances, with 3-monthly review
Severe scarring persisting a year after acne has cleared

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Counts of comedones, inflammatory lesions and nodules place the person in mild to moderate or moderate to severe acne.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Severity decides first-line treatment; assess scarring, pigmentary change and psychological impact at the same visit (NICE NG198, Terms used, Recs 1.4.3–1.4.4 and 1.5.1).
ruleIn.normalValue: Not applicable; NG198 gives no laboratory normal

ruleIn.testName: Assessment of psychological wellbeing and mental health history
ruleIn.targetCondition: Mental health disorder or distress related to acne
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Current or past suicidal ideation or self-harm, severe depressive or anxiety disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Ask in every consultation because acne of any severity can cause distress; mental health assessment is required before and monitoring during isotretinoin (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.5, 1.5.4, 1.5.21 and 1.5.26).

ruleIn.testName: Pregnancy test, fasting lipid profile and liver function before isotretinoin
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Venous blood or urine pregnancy test
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Pregnancy: do not prescribe. Abnormal lipids or liver function: assess risk before starting.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Pregnancy tests before prescribing, monthly during treatment, at the end of therapy and one month after stopping; fasting lipid profile and liver function tests before prescribing (FDA isotretinoin label, section 2.3). NICE requires following national regulator guidance and a pregnancy prevention programme for people who can become pregnant (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.22).
ruleIn.normalValue: Negative pregnancy test; lipid and liver values within local laboratory ranges (not defined in the sources)

references.title: NICE NG198: Acne vulgaris: management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendation 1.5.32

clinicalManagement.title: Assess, inform and screen for harm
actions: Give clear, tailored information on possible causes, treatment options, benefits and drawbacks, impact, adherence, relapse and when to seek advice (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.1.1).
Include parents and carers if the person wishes or needs support (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.1.2).
Take into account that acne of any severity can cause psychological distress and mental health disorders (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.4).
Consider a medical disorder or medication contributing to the acne (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.6).

clinicalManagement.title: Skin care and diet advice
actions: Use a non-alkaline synthetic detergent (syndet) cleanser twice daily on acne-prone skin (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.2.1).
Avoid oil-based and comedogenic skin care, sunscreens and make-up, and remove make-up at the end of the day (NICE NG198 Recs 1.2.2–1.2.3).
Advise that picking or scratching lesions can increase scarring risk (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.2.4).
Advise that there is not enough evidence to support specific diets (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.3.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Referral decisions
actions: Choose the referral urgency from the presentation (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.1–1.4.6).
Same-day referral to the on-call hospital dermatology team, assessed within 24 hours (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.1).

branches.condition: Diagnostic uncertainty, acne conglobata or nodulo-cystic acne
actions: Refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.2).

branches.condition: Failure of 2 courses (mild to moderate), failure with an oral antibiotic (moderate to severe), scarring, persistent pigmentary change, or persistent psychological distress
actions: Consider referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.3–1.4.4).

branches.condition: Significant psychological distress, suicidal ideation, self-harm, severe depression or anxiety, or body dysmorphic disorder
actions: Consider referral to mental health services, taking into account possible isotretinoin treatment (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.5).

clinicalManagement.title: First-line 12-week treatment
actions: Offer a 12-week course of one first-line option after discussing advantages and disadvantages (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.1). Do not use topical antibiotic alone, oral antibiotic alone, or topical plus oral antibiotic together (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.11).
To reduce irritation, start benzoyl peroxide or retinoid with alternate-day or short-contact application, then progress to standard use (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.7).

Cover pregnancy: topical retinoids and oral tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy and when planning pregnancy; effective contraception or an alternative is needed (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.8). If hormonal contraception is wanted, consider the combined pill over the progestogen-only pill (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.9).
Fixed combination adapalene with benzoyl peroxide once daily in the evening, or fixed combination tretinoin with clindamycin once daily in the evening (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.1 and Table 1).
Alternatively fixed combination benzoyl peroxide with clindamycin once daily in the evening (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.1 and Table 1).

Fixed combination adapalene with benzoyl peroxide once daily in the evening plus oral lymecycline or doxycycline once daily; or topical azelaic acid twice daily plus oral lymecycline or doxycycline once daily (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.1 and Table 1).
If oral lymecycline or doxycycline cannot be used, consider trimethoprim or an oral macrolide such as erythromycin (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.3).

branches.condition: Topical retinoid or antibiotic contraindicated or declined
actions: Consider benzoyl peroxide monotherapy (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Review at 12 weeks
actions: Assess improvement and side effects (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.12).

If an oral antibiotic is part of treatment: if cleared, consider stopping the antibiotic and continuing topical treatment; if improved but not cleared, consider continuing for up to 12 more weeks (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.12).
Continue an antibiotic-containing treatment beyond 6 months only in exceptional circumstances, with 3-monthly review (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.13).

Inadequate response: mild to moderate, offer another table option; moderate to severe without oral antibiotic, offer an option with one; moderate to severe with oral antibiotic, consider referral (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.16). Consider referral after 2 failed courses of mild to moderate acne (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.17).

clinicalManagement.title: Oral isotretinoin (specialist-led)
actions: Consider for severe acne in people older than 12 resistant to adequate courses of standard systemic antibiotic and topical therapy (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.18).

Follow the MHRA risk minimisation measures; counsel and monitor mental health and sexual function; use the regulatory documents (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.19). The people who can become pregnant need the pregnancy prevention programme (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.22).

Dose 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily; below 0.5 mg/kg if at increased risk of adverse effects; continue to a cumulative 120 to 150 mg/kg or stop sooner after 4 to 8 weeks with no new lesions (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.23–1.5.25).
Review psychological wellbeing during treatment and stop and seek urgent advice if mental health or sexual function problems are severe (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.26).
Consider oral prednisolone if a flare occurs after starting, or at the start for acne fulminans (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.27–1.5.28).

clinicalManagement.title: Other treatment options and scarring
actions: PMOS: first-line treatment first; if not effective consider ethinylestradiol with cyproterone acetate (co-cyprindiol) or another combined pill, reviewing co-cyprindiol at 6 months (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.31).
Consider photodynamic therapy for people 18 and over with moderate to severe acne if other treatments are ineffective, not tolerated or contraindicated (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.29).
Relapse: another 12-week course of the same or an alternative treatment; after isotretinoin, offer a table option, or re-refer for moderate to severe relapse (NICE NG198 Recs 1.6.1–1.6.4).
Maintenance: consider adapalene with benzoyl peroxide in people who relapse frequently, reviewing after 12 weeks (NICE NG198 Recs 1.7.3–1.7.5).
Severe scarring persisting a year after clearing: refer to a dermatology team with scarring expertise, which may consider CO2 laser or glycolic acid peel (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.8.2).

regimens.indication: Acne of any severity, first line
regimens.dose: 0.1% adapalene with 2.5% benzoyl peroxide, or 0.3% adapalene with 2.5% benzoyl peroxide (NICE NG198, Terms used)
adjustments: Start with alternate-day or short-contact application to reduce irritation, then progress (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.7)
Not for use in pregnancy; use with caution in breastfeeding (NICE NG198 Table 1)
monitoring: Skin irritation, photosensitivity, bleaching of hair and fabrics (NICE NG198 Table 1)
contraindications: Not for use in pregnancy (NICE NG198 Table 1)
FDA label for the 0.1%/2.5% gel lists no contraindications (section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendation 1.5.1 and Table 1; FDA label: Adapalene and benzoyl peroxide gel 0.1%/2.5% (set ID 049ea4d9-c60e-4406-b199-da5abe92eced)

regimens.indication: Moderate to severe acne, oral component
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with moderate to severe acne
regimens.dose: 100 mg doxycycline daily, or 408 mg lymecycline daily (NICE NG198, Terms used)
regimens.duration: 12-week course; extend up to 12 more weeks if improved but not cleared; beyond 6 months only exceptionally with 3-monthly review (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.12–1.5.13)
adjustments: Always combine with topical adapalene and benzoyl peroxide, or azelaic acid; never as monotherapy (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.1 and 1.5.11)
The US label dose of 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg/day is for infections, not acne
monitoring: Photosensitivity, systemic side effects and antimicrobial resistance (NICE NG198 Table 1)
contraindications: Contraindicated in pregnancy and when planning pregnancy; not for use under the age of 12 or during breastfeeding (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.8 and Table 1)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendations 1.5.1, 1.5.8 and 1.5.12–1.5.13, Terms used; FDA label: Doxycycline hyclate tablets (set ID 0106a3d3-db4d-f6ee-e063-6294a90a25e9)

regimens.indication: Moderate to severe acne, topical alternative
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with moderate to severe acne
regimens.genericName: Azelaic acid (with oral doxycycline or lymecycline)
regimens.dose: 15% or 20% azelaic acid (NICE NG198, Terms used)
adjustments: Combine with oral lymecycline or doxycycline (NICE NG198 Table 1)
monitoring: Reassess the diagnosis if there is no improvement after 12 weeks (FDA azelaic acid gel label; that label may be for another indication)
contraindications: Not for use in pregnancy or during breastfeeding in the NICE table combination with an oral tetracycline (NICE NG198 Table 1)
The FDA azelaic acid gel label lists no contraindications (section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendation 1.5.1 and Table 1; FDA label: Azelaic acid gel (set ID 0b5ab22e-c78a-4429-9a76-a4ba2d11fcde)

regimens.indication: Severe acne resistant to standard therapy
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe acne, under specialist care
regimens.dose: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.23); the FDA label says 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 15 to 20 weeks, up to 2 mg/kg/day for very severe adult disease
regimens.frequency: Daily (NICE); twice daily in divided doses, once-daily dosing not recommended (FDA label)
regimens.duration: Until a cumulative dose of 120 to 150 mg/kg (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.25); FDA label: 15 to 20 weeks
adjustments: Below 0.5 mg/kg for people at increased risk of, or experiencing, adverse effects (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.24)
FDA label: second course only after at least 2 months off therapy; if nodule count has fallen by more than 70% the course may stop early
monitoring: Mental health and sexual function reviewed during treatment (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.26)
Monthly pregnancy tests; fasting lipids and liver function before prescribing (FDA label section 2.3)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to isotretinoin, vitamin A or any component (FDA label section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026, Recommendations 1.5.18–1.5.26; FDA label: Isotretinoin capsules (set ID 08529687-26b2-41e5-b6fb-35b4c0d891fe)

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG198 gives formulations and doses for first-line options in its Terms used section; clindamycin combinations, tretinoin and lymecycline have no FDA label read here. Check SFDA registration, the SFDA isotretinoin prescribing requirements and the hospital formulary.

learningObjectives: Grade acne by lesion counts and choose a first-line 12-week option.
Avoid antibiotic monotherapy and limit antibiotic duration.
Recognise urgent and routine referral triggers and the safety requirements of isotretinoin.
keyPoints: Mild to moderate: up to 34 inflammatory lesions or up to 2 nodules; moderate to severe: 35 or more or 3 or more nodules.
First-line courses last 12 weeks; benefit takes 6 to 8 weeks to appear.
Never use topical or oral antibiotic as monotherapy, or topical plus oral antibiotic together.
pitfalls: Prescribing oral or topical antibiotic alone (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.11).
Continuing antibiotic-containing treatment beyond 6 months without exceptional reasons (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.13).
Using topical retinoids or oral tetracyclines in pregnancy (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.8).
Overlooking mental health risk before and during isotretinoin (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.21 and 1.5.26).
Stopping topical treatment at 12 weeks when frequent relapse suggests maintenance treatment (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.7.3).

references.title: NICE NG198: Acne vulgaris: management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 25 June 2021, last updated 3 August 2026
references.locator: Recommendations 1.1.1–1.8.2, Table 1 and Terms used in this guideline

patientEducation: Explain the possible causes, treatment options with benefits and drawbacks, impact of acne, adherence, and what to do if it relapses (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.1.1).
Explain that treatment effects take 6 to 8 weeks to be noticeable and that the course should be completed (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.5).
Counsel people who can become pregnant about retinoids, tetracyclines and isotretinoin (NICE NG198 Recs 1.5.8 and 1.5.22).
Explain that persistent picking or scratching can cause scarring (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.2.4).
After treatment, explain that maintenance treatment is not always necessary (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.7.2).
lifestyleAndDiet: Use a syndet cleanser twice daily and non-comedogenic products (NICE NG198 Recs 1.2.1–1.2.3).
Specific diets are not supported by enough evidence; general balanced-diet advice applies (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.3.1).
mdtReferrals: Consultant dermatologist-led team for the indications in NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.1–1.4.4.
Mental health services for significant distress, suicidal ideation or self-harm, severe depression or anxiety, or body dysmorphic disorder (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.4.5).
Reproductive endocrinologist or other specialist for contributing medical disorder or PMOS with hyperandrogenism (NICE NG198 Recs 1.4.6 and 1.5.32).
dischargeCriteria: Acne cleared with a plan for skin care and, if frequent relapse, maintenance treatment (NICE NG198 Recs 1.7.1–1.7.4).
Person knows when and how to get further advice and the treatment options if a relapse occurs (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.1.1).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 12 weeks for response and side effects (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.12). Review maintenance treatment after 12 weeks (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.7.5). For isotretinoin, monitor mental health and sexual function throughout the course (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.5.26). Refer severe scarring that persists a year after clearing (NICE NG198 Rec. 1.8.2).
